1.title: Controlling a Stage in Context
1.text: Welcome to Module thirteen: Controlling a Stage in Context. It covers the exam area The prince two processes. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. four point four.one apply controlling a stage: activities, inputs and outputs, roles and responsibilities, how the practices are applied. four point four.two analyze whether the activities, roles and responsibilities are effective and fit for purpose, considering tailoring, the practices, and the purpose and objectives of the process. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: The prince two processes (thirty percent). Exam format: an open-book scenario exam: one hundred fifty minutes, seventy marks, forty-two marks to pass. Validated against: the official prince two seven Practitioner syllabus (people cert), version seven point two.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves
1.text: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves. Controlling a stage is the process the project manager uses every day inside a delivery stage. The figure shows the cycle.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves, continued
1.text: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves. The figure shows this: Controlling a stage: the project manager authorizes work packages, reviews reports from team managers, reports to the board and escalates exceptions.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves, continued
1.text: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves. Purpose: assign work, monitor it, deal with issues, report progress to the board and take corrective action so that the stage stays within tolerance. Objectives: work is authorized and agreed first; progress is monitored; issues and risks are handled or escalated; the board is kept informed.

1.title: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves, continued
1.text: Purpose, objectives and the principles it serves. Manage by exception. The project manager acts inside tolerance and escalates only forecast breaches. Focus on products. Work packages ask for products with quality criteria. Define roles, responsibilities and relationships. The project manager controls, team managers deliver, the board directs. Continued business justification. Every issue and risk is checked for its effect on the business case. Exam tip: If a problem can be corrected inside the stage tolerance, the project manager corrects it and reports it in the next highlight report. Asking the board to decide something inside tolerance breaks manage by exception.

1.title: Activities, inputs and outputs
1.text: Activities, inputs and outputs. The names below give the general idea; check the Official Book's wording for the activities. Authorize work packages. Agrees work with team managers: products, tolerances, quality, reporting. Review work package status. Reads checkpoint reports and compares progress with the work package. Receive completed work packages. Confirms products are delivered, checked and approved. Review the stage status. Compares actuals with the stage plan and forecasts time, cost, scope and benefits. Report highlights. Sends the board a highlight report at the agreed interval.

1.title: Activities, inputs and outputs, continued
1.text: Activities, inputs and outputs. Capture and examine issues and risks. Records them and assesses the effect on the stage and the business case. Take corrective action. Acts inside tolerance to bring work back to plan. Escalate issues and risks. Raises anything beyond tolerance or authority to the board.

1.title: Activities, inputs and outputs, continued
1.text: Activities, inputs and outputs. Inputs from the board. Authorization of the stage, the approved stage plan, decisions and advice. Inputs from team managers. Checkpoint reports, completed work packages, quality records. Outputs to team managers. Authorized work packages. Outputs to the board. Highlight reports; exception reports; requests for advice or decisions. Outputs to the records. Updated stage plan, registers, daily log, lessons log. Exam tip: Work starts only through an authorized work package. If an option has a team starting from a chat, a meeting or the stage plan alone, it is not an effective approach.

1.title: Roles
1.text: Roles. Project manager. Responsible: authorizes work, monitors, reports, corrects, escalates. Team manager. Delivers work packages, sends checkpoint reports, raises issues and risks. Project board. Informed by highlight reports; advises; decides when an exception is escalated. Executive. Owns the business case; acts when the stage's justification is at risk. Senior user and senior supplier. Provide user and supplier resources; help solve problems in their area. Project assurance. Checks progress, risks and quality independently for the board. Change authority. Decides changes inside its delegated authority. Project support. Keeps the logs and registers; helps collect progress data.

1.title: Roles, continued
1.text: Roles. Check the book's roles table for this process. The general rule: the project manager is responsible, the board is informed and decides only on escalation, and team managers report to the project manager, not to the board.

1.title: How the practices are applied
1.text: How the practices are applied. Business case. Check each issue, risk and change for its effect on benefits and cost. Organization. Work flows through the agreed team structure and roles. Plans. The stage plan is the baseline; each work package carries tolerances. Quality. Work packages include product descriptions; quality records are reviewed. Risk. Review the risk register each cycle; act early; escalate what is beyond tolerance. Issues. Capture and examine, then send to the right authority: project manager, change authority or board. Progress. Reports, forecasts, tolerances and escalation by exception.

1.title: Judging a scenario
1.text: Judging a scenario. Work authorized through work packages that state products, tolerances, quality and reporting. Work starts from a verbal request, or the team sets its own scope. Tolerances watched and forecasts updated at every review. Reviews look only at past actuals, so a breach is seen too late. Exception report as soon as a breach is forecast. A breach is hidden, fixed quietly or left for the next highlight report. Corrective action inside tolerance taken by the project manager. The board is asked to decide routine matters inside tolerance.

1.title: Judging a scenario, continued
1.text: Judging a scenario. Issues and risks examined for their effect on the business case. A change is accepted without checking cost and benefit. The project manager keeps control while team managers deliver. Control is delegated to a team manager or supplier. Lessons captured as they arise. Lessons left until the end of the project.

2.title: Judging a scenario, continued
2.text: Judging a scenario. Tailoring changes the form, never the control. Agile teams: a work package can be an iteration. The team plans its own tasks, but the project manager still agrees outcomes, tolerances and reporting. Small projects: fewer documents and short verbal updates, if the board agrees first. Keep the record in the daily log. Large or multi-supplier projects: many team managers, a common report format, project support to consolidate. Sustainability, digital and data: track sustainability targets and use tool data, following the digital and data management approach. Exam tip: Tailoring lightens the form, never the control. An answer that drops authorization, tolerances or escalation fails. A shorter report the board agreed to can pass.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. In the build stage of Project Harbor, Wei Chen forecasts that one work package will finish three days late. The stage is still forecast to finish well inside its two-week time tolerance. Sam Okafor sends the board an exception report. Was this an appropriate action for the project manager to take, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: No, because the project manager can correct this inside the stage tolerance. The stage stays in tolerance, so the project manager takes corrective action and reports it in the highlight report (manage by exception).

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Sam Okafor sends Wei Chen's team a short message: build the permit form soon and keep the cost reasonable. It names no tolerances, quality criteria or reporting. Was this an appropriate action for the project manager to take, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: No, because the work package should state products, tolerances and quality. A work package is how work is authorized, so it must give the products, tolerances, quality and reporting for the team manager to agree.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. Project Harbor's build stage has a cost tolerance of plus or minus ten percent. Sam Okafor's latest forecast shows the stage finishing twelve percent over budget. What should Sam do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Raise an exception report to the board with options and a recommendation. A forecast breach of stage tolerance is an exception, so the project manager escalates promptly and the board decides.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. In the build stage of Project Harbor, a checkpoint report shows one product slipping by two days. The stage stays inside its tolerance. Who decides on the corrective action for the stage? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Sam Okafor, the project manager. Day-to-day control inside tolerance belongs to the project manager, and the board is not asked to decide.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Marta Quinn asks for a short, regular summary of build stage progress, issues and risks instead of attending frequent meetings. Which management product should Sam use? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: Highlight report. The highlight report goes from the project manager to the board at regular intervals.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A small internal project at Brightwater Port Authority has no team manager. The board agrees that the project manager gives a twenty-minute weekly verbal update and records actions in the daily log instead of written highlight reports. Was this appropriate tailoring, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Yes, because the board agreed a lighter form and stays informed. Tailoring may lighten the form of reports when the board agrees and still gets the information it needs.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the purpose of controlling a stage? Answer: To assign work, monitor it, handle issues, report progress and take corrective action so the stage stays within tolerance. Question two. Who is responsible for the controlling a stage process? Answer: The project manager. Question three. Which report does the project manager send to the board at regular intervals? Answer: The highlight report.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What must the project manager do when a stage is forecast to exceed its tolerance? Answer: Escalate to the project board with an exception report. Question five. Who sets the tolerances for a work package? Answer: The project manager sets them, and the team manager agrees them when accepting the work package. Question six. Which principle is the main one behind this process? Answer: Manage by exception.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Purpose: assign work, monitor, report, correct, keep the stage within tolerance. Activities: authorize, review, receive, report highlights, capture issues and risks, correct, escalate. Inputs: stage plan, checkpoint reports, completed work packages, board decisions. Outputs: authorized work packages, highlight reports, exception reports, updated logs. Effective: work packages, tolerances watched, early escalation, control kept. Red flags: verbal work, hidden breaches, board decides routine matters, delegated control. Tailoring: lighter form, never lighter control.
